_link.title: I can differentiate between open and closed systems

toLevel2.stem: What type of system allows both energy and matter to transfer between the reaction and its surroundings?
In a closed system, which of the following can transfer between the reaction and its surroundings?
Which of the following is an example of an open system?
toLevel2.answer: A flask with a loose top
distractors: A flask with a sealed stopper

toLevel2.stem: What is prevented from leaving in a closed system?
A flask with a tightly sealed stopper is an example of which type of system?
An open system allows matter to transfer between the reaction and its surroundings.
A closed system prevents both energy and matter from leaving the reaction vessel.
An open system allows both {{blank:1}} and {{blank:2}} to transfer between the reaction and its surroundings.
A closed system allows {{blank:1}} transfer but prevents {{blank:2}} from escaping.
A flask with a {{blank:1}} top is an open system, while a flask with a tightly {{blank:2}} stopper is a closed system.

toLevel3.stem: Why can gas escape from an open system but not from a closed system?
toLevel3.answer: An open system permits matter transfer while a closed system does not
distractors: An open system has higher pressure than a closed system
A closed system has no gas particles inside it
An open system is always at a higher temperature

toLevel3.stem: A student heats a beaker of water with no lid. Which statement best describes this system?
toLevel3.answer: It is open because water vapour can escape into the surroundings
distractors: It is closed because the beaker contains the water
It is open because no energy is transferred
It is closed because heat cannot leave the beaker

toLevel3.stem: How does a closed system differ from an open system in terms of energy transfer?
distractors: Only a closed system allows energy transfer
Only an open system allows energy transfer

toLevel3.stem: Which statement best explains why the type of system matters when monitoring a reaction?
toLevel3.answer: It determines which measurement methods give valid results
distractors: It changes the products that are formed in the reaction
It determines the activation energy of the reaction
It alters the order of the chemical equation

toLevel3.stem: A sealed flask contains a reaction that produces carbon dioxide gas. What happens to the gas in this closed system?
toLevel3.answer: It remains trapped inside the flask
distractors: It escapes through the walls of the flask
It is absorbed by the liquid reactants
It is converted back into solid carbon

toLevel3.stem: Why is it incorrect to say that a closed system prevents all transfers with the surroundings?
toLevel3.answer: Because energy can still transfer in or out of a closed system
distractors: Because matter can still escape through tiny openings
Because closed systems do not exist in real experiments
Because gas particles can pass through solid walls

toLevel3.stem: If a reaction produces a gas in an open system, the total mass of the system will decrease over time.
In an open system, gas produced during a reaction can {{blank:1}} into the surroundings, whereas in a closed system it remains {{blank:2}}.
The type of system affects which {{blank:1}} methods are valid and how the reaction {{blank:2}} over time.
Both open and closed systems allow {{blank:1}} transfer, but only an {{blank:2}} system also allows matter transfer.

toLevel4.stem: A student measures the mass of a reaction flask over time and observes a steady decrease. What type of system is most likely being used?
toLevel4.answer: An open system producing a gas
distractors: A closed system producing a gas
An open system with no gas produced

toLevel4.stem: A teacher wants students to collect all gaseous products of a reaction. Which system should they use?
toLevel4.answer: A closed system so no gas escapes
distractors: An open system so gas can be observed
An open system to prevent pressure build-up
A closed system to stop energy transfer

toLevel4.stem: Calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid in an open beaker. Which observation would confirm the system is open?
toLevel4.answer: The mass on the balance decreases as gas escapes
distractors: The temperature of the solution increases

toLevel4.stem: A student seals a flask and runs a gas-producing reaction. What happens to the total mass of the flask and its contents?
An experiment requires measuring the volume of gas produced over time. Which setup is most appropriate?
toLevel4.answer: A closed system connected to a gas syringe
distractors: An open beaker on a balance
An open flask with a thermometer
A sealed flask with no outlet

toLevel4.stem: In an experiment, a student notices that mass is conserved throughout a gas-producing reaction. What does this indicate about the system?
A reaction produces water vapour. In which system type would measuring mass loss be a valid way to monitor the reaction rate?
If a gas-producing reaction takes place in an open system, the {{blank:1}} of the system will decrease because {{blank:2}} escapes.
To accurately measure all products of a reaction, a {{blank:1}} system should be used to prevent {{blank:2}} from escaping.
Measuring mass loss over time is a valid method for monitoring reaction rate in an {{blank:1}} system, but not in a {{blank:2}} system where gas cannot escape.

toLevel5.stem: A student measures the mass of an open flask during a reaction and finds it decreases by 2.2 g. They repeat the experiment in a sealed flask and the mass stays constant. What explains the difference?
toLevel5.answer: Gas produced in the open system escaped, while in the closed system it was retained
distractors: The sealed flask prevented the reaction from occurring
More product was formed in the sealed flask
The open system absorbed matter from the surroundings

toLevel5.stem: Two identical reactions are run, one in an open beaker and one in a sealed flask. Both are placed on balances. Which result would indicate a gas-producing reaction?
toLevel5.answer: The open beaker shows decreasing mass while the sealed flask shows constant mass
distractors: Both show decreasing mass over time
Both show constant mass over time
The sealed flask shows increasing mass while the open beaker shows constant mass

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that mass is not conserved in an open system because the balance reading decreases during a gas-producing reaction. Is this claim valid?
toLevel5.answer: No, mass is conserved overall but some matter has left the system as gas
distractors: Yes, mass is genuinely destroyed in open systems
Yes, the decrease proves that atoms are lost
No, the balance must be malfunctioning

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that monitoring mass loss is always the best method for measuring reaction rate. Which situation would challenge this claim?
toLevel5.answer: A reaction in a closed system where no mass leaves
distractors: A reaction that produces a large volume of gas
A reaction that releases a lot of heat energy
A reaction that uses a solid catalyst

toLevel5.stem: In an experiment, a student measures the volume of gas collected in a gas syringe connected to a sealed flask. Why would this method fail in a completely open system?
toLevel5.answer: Gas would escape into the surroundings instead of entering the syringe
distractors: An open system does not produce any gas
The syringe cannot function without a sealed flask
Gas volume cannot be measured at atmospheric pressure

toLevel5.stem: A student suggests converting an open system to a closed system by simply placing a cotton wool plug in the flask opening. Evaluate this approach.
toLevel5.answer: It reduces matter loss but may not fully prevent gas from escaping through the cotton wool
distractors: It creates a perfectly sealed closed system
It has no effect on whether matter can escape
It prevents both energy and matter from leaving

toLevel5.stem: A reaction in an open system appears to slow down over time. Which factor related to the system type could contribute to this observation?
toLevel5.answer: Gaseous reactants or products escaping reduce the concentration of reacting particles
distractors: Energy cannot enter the system to sustain the reaction
The open system prevents collisions between particles
The temperature automatically decreases in open systems

toLevel5.stem: A student plans to compare reaction rates by measuring mass loss in two experiments: one in an open beaker and one in a sealed flask. Why is this comparison flawed?
toLevel5.answer: The sealed flask will show no mass loss regardless of reaction rate, making comparison invalid
distractors: Mass loss is never a valid method for measuring reaction rate
The sealed flask will always show a faster reaction rate
The open beaker will not produce any gas for measurement

toLevel5.stem: When comparing the same reaction in open and closed systems, the {{blank:1}} system shows a mass decrease because gaseous products {{blank:2}} into the surroundings.
Measuring gas volume with a syringe requires a {{blank:1}} system so that all gas produced is {{blank:2}} rather than lost to the surroundings.
